raw_case_text:
A 15-month-old boy presented with complains of pain, redness and photophobia in the left eye since 2 months. There was a vague history of trauma, following which the parents noticed the symptoms. The child was healthy with normal developmental milestones and was well immunized for age. Visual acuity could not be assessed due to extreme photophobia. The left eye had diffuse corneal haze with blood staining. There was circumciliary congestion and anterior chamber showed hyphema obstructing the fundus view. The intraocular pressure was 26 mmHg. The other eye was normal. Ultrasound B-scan showed few low reflective dot echoes with an attached retina with no evidence of any intraocular foreign body, mass lesion or calcification. With a working diagnosis of post-traumatic hyphema with secondary glaucoma, the child was started on topical antiglaucoma and cycloplegics. But the condition of the child acutely worsened within a week. The left eye progressed to proptosis, lid edema and restriction of movement. Anterior chamber was filled with blood tinged fibrinous exudates and a scleral abscess was noted at the infero-temporal limbus [Figure 1]. Repeat B-scan revealed plenty of medium reflective membranous echoes with collection of sub-Tenons fluid (positive T sign).
CT-scan orbit revealed proptosis with increased preseptal soft tissue edema. Multiple hyperdense membranes/septae were seen in the mid and posterior vitreous suggestive of multiple abscess in the vitreous. Increased thickening of the sclera and choroid was noted. There was no evidence of an intraocular mass lesion or calcification. On IV contrast, there was a ring enhancing lesion in the intraconal space just behind the globe suggestive of an intraconal abscess [Figure 3a and b]. A diagnosis of panophthalmitis was made and a pediatrician consult was sought to rule out any systemic foci of infection for endogenous etiology. Systemic examination and investigations were negative.
As there was no improvement in the eye condition after 24 h of systemic broad spectrum antibiotics, evisceration was planned. Intraocular contents were sent for microbiology and histopathologic evaluation.
On Gram stains, mildly Gram-positive beaded filaments more prominent in the modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain with 1% sulphuric acid were noted [Figure 2a and b]. Chalky white colonies grew on the Chocolate agar 3 days after inoculation [Figure 2c]. Smear from culture confirmed the presence of Nocardia. Based on the sensitivity pattern the patient was started on oral combination of Sulphamethoxazole (8 mg/kg/day) + Trimethoprim (50 mg/kg/day) along with topical Moxifloxacin. The child had a healthy socket with no evidence of local recurrence at 1 week and 1 month follow-up. The antibiotics were continued for 10 weeks. He showed no signs of systemic or local recurrence till his last follow-up at 1 year.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 15-month-old boy presented with a 2-month history of left eye pain, redness, and extreme photophobia following vague ocular trauma.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: Two months prior to presentation, the infant's parents noticed left eye pain, redness, and severe photophobia following a vague history of trauma. Initially treated with topical antiglaucoma and cycloplegic drops for presumed post-traumatic hyphema with secondary glaucoma, the left eye acutely worsened within 1 week with proptosis, eyelid edema, restricted extraocular motility, blood-tinged fibrinous anterior chamber exudates, and an inferotemporal limbal scleral abscess unresponsive to 24 hours of systemic broad-spectrum antibiotics.
subjective.past_medical_history: Healthy 15-month-old toddler with normal developmental milestones and up-to-date immunizations; vague history of left ocular trauma 2 months prior.

objective.physical_examination: Initial left eye exam showed extreme photophobia precluding visual acuity testing, circumciliary congestion, diffuse corneal haze with blood staining, hyphema obstructing the fundus view, and elevated intraocular pressure of 26 mmHg (right eye normal). One week later, the left eye exhibited proptosis, lid edema, restricted extraocular movements, anterior chamber filled with blood-tinged fibrinous exudates, and a scleral abscess at the inferotemporal limbus. Pediatric systemic examination was normal.
objective.routine_investigations: Initial B-scan ocular ultrasound showed a few low-reflective dot echoes with an attached retina and no intraocular foreign body, mass, or calcification; repeat B-scan at 1 week showed numerous medium-reflective membranous echoes and sub-Tenon's fluid collection (positive T-sign). Systemic pediatric investigations were negative.
objective.advanced_workup: Contrast-enhanced orbital CT revealed left proptosis, preseptal soft-tissue edema, multiple hyperdense vitreous membranes/septae suggestive of intravitreal abscesses, scleral and choroidal thickening, and a ring-enhancing intraconal abscess immediately posterior to the globe without intraocular mass or calcification. Left ocular evisceration was performed.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Exogenous post-traumatic left panophthalmitis and intraconal orbital abscess caused by Nocardia spp. in a 15-month-old child was confirmed on eviscerated intraocular contents: Gram stain showed mildly Gram-positive beaded filaments, modified Ziehl-Neelsen stain (1% H2SO4) showed acid-fast beaded branching filaments, and chocolate agar culture grew chalky-white colonies after 3 days. Following left eye evisceration, susceptibility-guided therapy with oral trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole (TMP-SMX, 8/50 mg/kg/day) and topical moxifloxacin for 10 weeks resulted in a healthy socket without local or systemic recurrence at 1-week, 1-month, and 1-year follow-up.
